meta.blurb: A cursed family, a monstrous hound and a lonely moor. When Sir Henry Baskerville inherits his ancestors' house, only Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson can learn whether the beast is a ghost or something more human. Can they stop it in time?
meta.bible: Sherlock Holmes: the great London detective, calm, sharp, and fond of surprises. Dr Watson: his friend and the narrator's point of view, loyal and honest. Dr Mortimer: a kind country doctor and friend of Sir Charles. Sir Henry Baskerville: the young heir, newly arrived from Canada. Sir Charles Baskerville: Sir Henry's uncle, who died on the yew path at Baskerville Hall; weak heart. Hugo Baskerville: a cruel ancestor in the old manuscript. Barrymore: the butler at Baskerville Hall. Mrs Barrymore: his wife; her younger brother is the convict Selden. Jack Stapleton: a naturalist who collects butterflies near Merripit House; really a Baskerville and the villain. Beryl Stapleton: Jack's wife, who pretends to be his sister. Laura Lyons: a woman of Coombe Tracey who wrote to Sir Charles. Mr Frankland: a quarrelsome old neighbour with a telescope. Selden: the escaped convict, killed in Sir Henry's old clothes. Inspector Lestrade: the Scotland Yard detective. Baskerville Hall: the old family house. Grimpen Mire: the dangerous bog on the moor. Dartmoor: the wild moor. Devonshire: the county. Merripit House: the Stapletons' house. Coombe Tracey: the village where Laura Lyons lives. Baker Street: where Holmes lives. London. Canada. Scotland Yard. Voice and tone: tense, clear and clever, a mystery told step by step; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore; the hound is a real dog covered in glowing phosphorus, not a ghost.

A1A2: Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson found a walking stick in their room.
Holmes looked at the stick and told Watson many things about its owner.
Dr Mortimer came to Baker Street for his stick and for Holmes's help.
Dr Mortimer read an old paper about Hugo Baskerville, a very cruel man.
Hugo locked up a girl, but she ran away across the dark moor.
Later his friends found Hugo dead beside a huge black hound.
Sir Charles Baskerville died on a dark path, and people spoke of the curse.
Near the body, Dr Mortimer saw the huge footprints of a dog.
Sir Henry Baskerville came from Canada and showed Holmes a strange letter.
Someone took a new boot from the hotel, then took an old boot.
A man with a beard followed Sir Henry in a cab through London.
Holmes was too busy to go, so he sent Watson with Sir Henry.
At the little station, soldiers were looking for a prisoner called Selden.
Baskerville Hall was big and dark, and Barrymore the butler welcomed them.
At night Watson heard a woman crying in the great house.
Stapleton, a man with a butterfly net, showed Watson the dangerous Grimpen Mire.
That evening a terrible cry came across the moor, and Watson felt afraid.
Beryl Stapleton ran to Watson and said, “Go back to London at once!”
Sir Henry liked Beryl very much, but her brother was not happy.
One night Watson saw Barrymore holding a candle at a window.
Barrymore said the candle was a signal for Selden, his wife's brother.
Watson and Sir Henry went out onto the moor to catch Selden.
On a rock above them, they saw a tall man standing alone.
Barrymore also found a burned letter from a woman to Sir Charles.
Mr Frankland watched the moor all day through his big telescope.
Laura Lyons told Watson that she asked Sir Charles to meet her.
She never went to the meeting, because someone told her to stay at home.
Frankland saw a boy carry food to a hidden man on the moor.
Watson climbed a rocky hill and found some small stone houses.
Inside, there was a bed, some food, and a letter about Watson himself.
Watson was amazed because the man in the hut was Sherlock Holmes.
Holmes had come in secret to watch the moor and the people there.
They heard a scream and found a dead man in Sir Henry's old clothes.
It was Selden, and then Stapleton arrived and looked shocked to see Holmes.
Holmes saw an old painting of Hugo, and the face was like Stapleton's.
Inspector Lestrade came from London, and Holmes told him a clever plan.
The three men hid near Merripit House while a thick fog came in.
Sir Henry left the house alone, and he walked home through the fog.
A huge hound jumped out of the fog, and its mouth shone with fire.
Holmes fired his gun, and the great hound fell down dead.
The hound was only a big dog covered in shining paint.
Stapleton had tied up Beryl, and the men found her in the house.
Stapleton ran away across the moor toward the Mire in the dark.
Holmes followed his footprints to the Mire and found a lost boot.
Holmes said Stapleton was a Baskerville, and he wanted the family house and money.
Stapleton used the hound to scare Sir Charles, and the old man died.
Sir Henry felt weak after that night, but his friends took care of him.
Later Sir Henry and Dr Mortimer took a long trip around the world.
Holmes and Watson went back to London, and the case was closed.
That evening in Baker Street, Holmes asked Watson to go to the opera.
B1B2: A walking stick has been left behind in Baker Street, and Sherlock Holmes studies it closely. Dr Watson is sure that his friend will soon learn a great deal from it.
Holmes says that the owner is a kind country doctor who walks a lot and owns a small dog. Watson is amazed, although he has seen his friend do such things many times before.
A tall, worried man knocks at the door and asks if anyone has seen his stick. It is Dr Mortimer, and he has come to Holmes because of a very strange problem.
Dr Mortimer takes out an old paper and reads it aloud by lamplight. It tells of Hugo Baskerville, a cruel and wild man who once lived at Baskerville Hall.
Hugo locked up a farmer's daughter in an upstairs room, but she escaped through a window and ran onto the moor. Hugo and his drunken friends jumped on their horses and rode after her.
At last his friends found Hugo dead on the moor, with an enormous black hound standing over him. Since that night, the story says, a curse has followed every Baskerville.
Dr Mortimer then says that his friend Sir Charles Baskerville has recently died on a path lined with yew trees. People in the village are saying that the family curse has finally caught him.

Near the body, Mortimer noticed the footprints of an enormous dog, though nobody else paid any attention to them. Holmes listens carefully, because he wants to know why such a kind old man suddenly died.

The next morning Sir Henry Baskerville, the new owner of the Hall, arrives from Canada and shows Holmes a strange letter. It warns him to keep away from the moor, and its words have been cut out of a newspaper.
While Sir Henry stays at his hotel, someone steals a new brown boot from outside his door. The next night an old black boot disappears as well, which makes no sense to anyone.
A man with a black beard has been following Sir Henry in a cab all around London. Holmes hurries after him, but the cab disappears into the busy traffic and nobody learns his name.
Holmes cannot leave London because of another important case, so he decides to send Watson to Devonshire instead. Watson must stay close to Sir Henry and write to Holmes about everything he sees.

At the small station near Dartmoor, soldiers are searching the fields because a dangerous prisoner called Selden has escaped. The travellers drive on through the dusk, and the lonely hills look dark and cold.
Baskerville Hall stands at the end of a long, dark avenue, and its grey walls look cold. Barrymore the butler and his wife welcome them politely, but both seem uneasy.
In the middle of the night, Watson wakes up and hears someone crying softly somewhere in the house. In the morning, Mrs Barrymore's eyes are red, but she says nothing.

On the moor, Watson meets a friendly naturalist called Jack Stapleton, who is chasing butterflies with a net. Stapleton warns him to stay away from Grimpen Mire, because a single wrong step there can mean death.
As the sun goes down, a long, deep howl rolls across the moor and makes Watson's blood run cold. Stapleton says that it is only a bird, but he does not look very sure.
Beryl Stapleton hurries over the grass, mistakes Watson for Sir Henry, and begs him to leave Devonshire at once. A moment later she realises her mistake and walks away, looking frightened.
Sir Henry soon falls in love with Beryl, but her brother Jack does not like it and angrily tells him to keep away. Watson cannot understand why Stapleton is so unhappy about a simple friendship.
One night Watson wakes and sees a light moving along the corridor upstairs. Following it quietly, he discovers Barrymore holding a candle at a window that looks toward the moor.

When Sir Henry and Watson ask him why, Barrymore admits that the candle is a signal for Selden, the escaped prisoner. Selden is Mrs Barrymore's younger brother, and the couple have been bringing him food.
Sir Henry wants to catch the prisoner, so the two men go out onto the moor at night. They soon see Selden's pale face in the moonlight, but he runs away across the rocks before they can reach him.
As they turn back, Watson sees a tall, thin man standing completely still on a rock against the moon. Before he can call out, the stranger vanishes, and the two friends are left alone with the wind.
Barrymore also hands over a scrap of burned paper that he found in Sir Charles's fireplace. Dr Mortimer says that the two initials on it must belong to Laura Lyons, who lives at Coombe Tracey.

Mr Frankland, a loud and quarrelsome old neighbour, loves going to court and spends his days at a telescope on his roof. Everyone in the district knows that he sees almost everything that happens on the moor.

Watson visits Laura Lyons at Coombe Tracey, and at first she refuses to say anything about Sir Charles. Finally she admits that she wrote to him, because she hoped that he would help her with her money problems.
She says that she asked Sir Charles to meet her at the gate that night, but she never went there. Someone she trusted told her to stay at home, although she will not say who it was.

On his way home, Watson meets Frankland, who says that a boy carries food to a hidden man on the moor. Frankland has watched the boy through his telescope, and he points to the rocky hill where the boy goes.
Watson decides to find the hidden man for himself, so he walks across the moor to the rocky hill. Old stone huts stand among the rocks there, and people lived in them thousands of years ago.
Inside one hut, Watson finds a blanket, some tins of food, and a note on a scrap of paper. Reading it, he is shocked to see that it describes his own visit to Coombe Tracey.
Footsteps come closer in the dark, and Watson waits behind a rock with his gun in his hand. Then a calm, familiar voice calls out, and Sherlock Holmes himself steps into the doorway, smiling.
Holmes explains that he has been living in the old hut so that he could watch the moor without being seen. He has learned that someone is trying to harm Sir Henry, and he has a good idea who it is.
A terrible scream breaks the silence of the night, and the two men run toward the sound. Among the rocks they find a body in Sir Henry's old clothes, and for a moment they fear the worst.

Holmes turns the body over and sees that the dead man is not Sir Henry but Selden, the escaped prisoner. Just then Stapleton hurries up, and he looks pale and very surprised to see Holmes standing there.
Back at the Hall, Holmes looks at an old painting of Hugo Baskerville for a very long time. Suddenly he sees that the cruel face has the same eyes and chin as Stapleton.
Inspector Lestrade arrives from London, and Holmes explains a plan to catch the villain. Sir Henry will dine at Merripit House and walk home across the moor, while the three men wait nearby.
On the chosen night, Holmes, Watson and Lestrade hide among the rocks near Merripit House. A thick white fog is rolling in from the Mire, and soon they can hardly see their own hands.
At last the door opens, and Sir Henry steps out and begins to walk home along the narrow path. The fog is already thick around him, and his footsteps sound very loud in the silence.
Suddenly a huge black hound leaps out of the fog, and its mouth and eyes seem to burn with fire. Sir Henry cries out and runs, and the terrible animal follows him.

Holmes runs forward and fires his revolver straight into the hound's side, and the huge animal rolls over with a howl. Sir Henry lies pale and shaking on the grass, but he is unhurt, and the hound will never harm anyone again.
Close up, the creature is not a ghost at all but a very large dog. Its mouth and coat have been rubbed with a chemical that glows in the dark, so it looks like a demon.
The men hurry into Merripit House, where they find Beryl tied up in a bedroom. Stapleton is not her brother but her husband, and he tied her up because she would not help his plan.
Stapleton himself is gone, and the only safe hiding place for him is a secret path through Grimpen Mire. Holmes and Watson run after him in the thick fog, but they cannot tell where the path leads.

In the morning, Holmes follows Stapleton's footprints to the edge of the Mire, where they end in soft green mud. Beside them lies Sir Henry's missing boot, and Holmes believes that the Mire has swallowed Stapleton, although nobody can ever prove it.

Holmes explains that Jack Stapleton was really a Baskerville, a nephew of Sir Charles and the next heir after Sir Henry. He wanted the Hall and the family fortune, so he planned to remove the two men who stood in his way.

Stapleton kept a huge dog hidden in the Mire and covered it with glowing paint to copy the hound of the legend. Sir Charles had a weak heart, and he died of fright when the beast ran toward him along the yew path.
Sir Henry is shaken and weak after his terrible night, and Dr Mortimer tells him to rest. Little by little, with the help of his friends, he begins to feel strong again.

When he is strong enough, Sir Henry decides to take a long sea voyage with Dr Mortimer, hoping to forget his fear. Before they go, he thanks Holmes and Watson warmly, because he knows that they have saved his life.
Holmes and Watson travel back to London on the train, tired but satisfied. Behind them, the people of Devonshire can walk on the moor again without fear of the hound.
On a foggy evening at Baker Street, Holmes puts down his pipe and suggests that they go to the opera. Watson laughs, glad to see his friend relaxed again after so many days of danger.
C1C2: Early one morning in Baker Street, a stranger's walking stick was discovered propped beside the door, and Sherlock Holmes seized upon it as though it were a letter written in his own language. Dr Watson, who had been watching his friend's growing delight over breakfast, waited for the performance he knew was coming. Few detectives in London could read a plain object so thoroughly, and none could do it with such unhurried pleasure.

With a flourish, Holmes announced that the stick's owner was a country doctor, respected by his neighbours and fond of a dog, since the marks of its teeth were plain upon the handle. Watson, who had long since given up trying to catch his friend in an error, listened with the mixture of wonder and irritation that these displays always produced. Every detail, however humble, seemed to confess to Holmes the history of the man who had carried it.

Their conversation was interrupted by a tall, stooping figure who hurried in without ceremony, anxiously scanning the room for the stick he had left behind. It was Dr Mortimer, a country doctor of gentle manners, and the strain in his face betrayed that he had come about more than a mislaid walking stick. He had travelled to Baker Street, he said, to lay before the great detective a matter that had troubled him for weeks.

Drawing a yellowed manuscript from his coat, Dr Mortimer settled beside the lamp and began to read in a low, steady voice. It told of Hugo Baskerville, a squire of savage temper and wicked habits, who had ruled Baskerville Hall in the days of the Civil War. Even the family's own chronicle, it seemed, admitted that no one in the neighbourhood had ever loved him, and few had dared to cross him.

One autumn night Hugo carried off a farmer's daughter, locked her in an upper room, and sat down with his drunken companions to feast below. The terrified girl, however, climbed from the window and fled across the dark moor toward her father's farm. When Hugo discovered her flight, he flew into a rage, called for his horse, and set off in pursuit with his companions at his heels.

At length the riders found the girl lying dead on the moor, worn out by terror and exhaustion, and Hugo himself lay lifeless beside her. Over his body, they swore, stood an enormous black hound, its eyes burning like coals, which fled howling into the night. From that day, the chronicle warned, the same shape had haunted the Baskervilles, and the family had lived in the shadow of its curse.

Dr Mortimer closed the manuscript and spoke more quietly, for he had come to the real reason for his visit. His friend and patient, Sir Charles Baskerville, had been found dead at the end of the yew alley beside the Hall, and the village already whispered that the old curse had claimed another victim. Sir Charles, a generous man with a weak heart, had gone out for his usual evening walk and never returned.

Mortimer then added the detail that he had mentioned to nobody else, that beside the body he had seen the footprints of an enormous dog. Holmes, who had been listening with his eyes half closed, sat suddenly upright and wished aloud that he had seen the scene himself. The matter, he declared, was far stranger and far more dangerous than a village legend, and he meant to look into it with great care.

The question was urgent, for Sir Henry Baskerville, the last of the line, had just arrived from Canada to claim the Hall, and Mortimer feared for his safety. Sir Henry, a frank and cheerful young man, came to Baker Street the next morning with a letter that had reached him at his hotel. Its words had been clipped from a newspaper and pasted onto a sheet, and they urged him, if he valued his life or his reason, to keep away from the moor.

Strange events multiplied almost at once, for during his first night in London a new brown boot vanished from outside Sir Henry's hotel room. The following night a different, much older boot disappeared in its place, and Sir Henry, who could not make sense of such trivial thefts, grew more irritated than frightened. Holmes, however, treated the matter with the utmost seriousness, as if the missing leather might lead him to the very heart of the mystery.

As they drove through the crowded streets, Holmes caught sight of a man with a thick black beard watching them from a passing cab. He sprang after the vehicle, but the cab was swallowed by the traffic, and the watcher escaped him. Nevertheless the cabman, when traced, reported that his passenger had given the name of Sherlock Holmes, a piece of impudence which the detective admired.

Duty kept Holmes in London, where another case demanded his attention, and he could not accompany his client to Devonshire at once. He therefore entrusted Watson with the task, instructing him never to leave Sir Henry alone on the moor after dark. Watson was to observe everything, report faithfully by letter, and trust nothing that he could not see for himself.

Their train carried them westward into Devonshire, and at a tiny station a line of soldiers peered across the fields, hunting for Selden, a convict who had escaped from the prison nearby. As the carriage rattled toward the Hall through the gathering dusk, the hills of Dartmoor rose around them, bleak, silent and strangely threatening. Sir Henry gazed out at the land of his ancestors with a curious mixture of excitement and unease.

Baskerville Hall appeared at last at the end of a long avenue of dark trees, its grey stone front glimmering faintly in the twilight. Barrymore the butler and his wife, Mrs Barrymore, received them in the great hall with grave courtesy, though both appeared curiously nervous. It was not the homecoming Sir Henry had imagined, and the gloom of the place settled upon all three men.

That night Watson lay awake in his old, panelled bedroom and, in the stillness between the striking of the hall clock, heard the unmistakable sound of a woman sobbing. The noise came from somewhere inside the house, muffled and bitter, and it stopped before he could track it to its source. At breakfast Mrs Barrymore's eyes were swollen with weeping, yet she answered every question with a blank denial.

On his first walk across the moor, Watson fell in with a slim, sunburnt naturalist named Jack Stapleton, who was racing after a butterfly with a net and an enthusiasm that disarmed all suspicion. Stapleton pointed out the green and innocent carpet of Grimpen Mire, where, he said, a single false step could swallow a man or a pony without a trace. He spoke of the place with a calm familiarity, as one speaks of an old acquaintance whose temper one knows well.

Dusk settled over the moor as they talked, and from somewhere far across the dark swell of the hills there rolled a long, low, mournful howl that made the hair rise on Watson's neck. Stapleton, whose face had changed for a moment, laughed it off and said that the sound was only some bird, or perhaps the groaning of the mire itself. Watson accepted the explanation politely, but he noticed that the naturalist's hand had trembled.

On another walk, Watson was startled by Beryl Stapleton, who came hurrying over the grass toward him, her face white and her words tumbling out too quickly to follow. She had mistaken him for Sir Henry, and she begged him, with desperate sincerity, to go back to London at once and never to return to the moor. Realising her error, she broke off, stammered something about a mistake, and hurried away across the heather without once looking behind her.

Sir Henry, meanwhile, had fallen headlong in love with Beryl, whose quiet beauty made a sharp contrast to the sombre moor. Her brother, as Jack Stapleton then appeared to be, took the courtship with open displeasure and begged the young heir to give it time. Watson, puzzled by so much anxiety over a harmless attachment, tucked the oddity away in his memory for later.

Late one night Watson woke to the sound of soft footsteps and, slipping into the corridor, saw a light moving stealthily along the upper floor. He followed it to the end of the passage, where Barrymore stood motionless at a window with a candle held high, gazing out over the black expanse of the moor. It was clearly a signal, and the butler's rigid attention suggested that he expected an answer.

When Sir Henry and Watson confronted him the following morning, Barrymore at first protested, then confessed that the candle was a signal to Selden, the escaped convict hiding on the moor. Selden, he admitted, was his wife's younger brother, and the couple had been secretly carrying food to him ever since he had broken out of prison. It was the sobbing that Watson had heard on his first night, for Mrs Barrymore was frantic with worry for the brother she could not abandon.

Sir Henry, though sympathetic to the pair, would not leave a dangerous man at large, and he and Watson set out across the moor that very night. The moon was bright, the rocks lay black on the silver grass, and presently a pale, wild face appeared among the stones, that of Selden himself. Before they could reach him, the convict bounded away over the boulders and was lost in the darkness.

As they turned back, Watson looked up and saw, outlined against the full moon on a distant crag, the figure of a tall, thin man standing perfectly still. The stranger seemed to be watching the moor like a sentry, and he was gone before Watson could cry out or raise his gun. In that moment Watson realised that the moor held another secret besides the convict, and one that was altogether more dangerous.

Barrymore had one more contribution to make, a scrap of burned paper that he had found in the grate of Sir Charles's study, bearing the faint ending of a woman's note. It asked the old gentleman to be at the gate at ten o'clock and to burn the message, and it was signed only with two initials. Dr Mortimer, when consulted, said that the letters must belong to Laura Lyons, a young woman who lived in Coombe Tracey.

In the neighbourhood no one was better known than Mr Frankland, a loud and quarrelsome old gentleman who loved nothing so much as a lawsuit. When he was not suing someone, he sat on the roof of his house with a telescope, sweeping the moor for anything that might furnish him with a grievance or a piece of gossip. Little, in consequence, escaped his notice, and Watson soon realised how useful that might be.

Determined to learn the truth, Watson drove to Coombe Tracey and called upon Laura Lyons, who received him with guarded politeness and refused at first to discuss Sir Charles at all. Under steady questioning, however, she admitted that she had written to him in desperate need of money, hoping that he would pity her circumstances and settle her debts. Her tone was defiant, yet Watson felt that she was keeping back far more than she told.

She had asked Sir Charles to meet her at the gate on the evening he died, she said, but she had never gone, for a friend had persuaded her to stay at home. Who that friend was she steadfastly declined to say, and Watson, watching her face, felt certain that the name would matter greatly. Sir Charles had waited alone at the gate, then, and had paced up and down the dark alley with no one to meet him.

Returning across the moor, Watson met Frankland again, who was beside himself with the pleasure of a discovery, for through his telescope he had seen a boy carrying a basket of food toward a distant hill. The lad went there every day, he insisted, and could only be feeding a hidden man, whom Frankland imagined to be the convict. Watson, who knew very well where the convict was getting his food, drew a quite different conclusion and thanked him gravely.

On the following evening Watson climbed the rocky hill himself, a bleak summit crowned with the roofless stone huts of some prehistoric people. He moved from hut to hut with his revolver in his pocket, listening to the wind and watching for any trace of the unknown man. Among all the ruins, one small dwelling looked far less abandoned than the rest, and its doorway was dark and silent.

Inside the hut Watson found a rolled blanket, a few tins of food, a water bottle, and, lying on a flat stone, a scrap of paper in a neat, unfamiliar hand. It read, in a few brief words, that Dr Watson had gone to Coombe Tracey. He stood quite still, understanding at last that someone had been following him through the whole of his private errands.

Footsteps then sounded outside, slow and unhurried, and Watson crouched in the shadows with his revolver cocked and his heart pounding. A voice that he knew better than any other in the world called out softly into the dark, and a tall figure stepped into the pale moonlit doorway. It was Sherlock Holmes, smiling at his friend's astonishment, and the whole mystery of the stranger on the tor fell into place.

Holmes explained that he had come down from London in secret, leaving Watson as the visible guardian while he himself lived unseen in the hut, where no enemy would think to look. He had read every one of Watson's reports with care, and he had gathered enough on his own to suspect a clever and ruthless hand behind the whole affair. The danger, he warned, was far from over, and Sir Henry, who suspected nothing, was still the intended victim of a patient and determined enemy.

Before they could talk further, a terrible scream rose out of the darkness, a cry of such agony that both men sprang up and ran toward it across the rocks. At the foot of a crag lay a body in Sir Henry's familiar old clothes, and for a dreadful moment they believed that they had come too late. Holmes knelt beside the body, struck a match, and drew a sharp breath as the small flame trembled over the dead man's face.

The face, in that small light, was not Sir Henry's but Selden's, for Barrymore had given the convict a bundle of his master's discarded garments. The man had fallen from the crag in his flight, and the dead body spoke of terror more than of violence. Just then a figure came hurrying through the heather, and Stapleton, with his net still in his hand, stopped dead and stared at Holmes with undisguised dismay.

Back at the Hall, Holmes lingered before the portraits of the Baskerville ancestors, until his eye settled upon a painting of Hugo in his cavalier dress. He covered the hat and the long hair with his hand, and the cruel, narrow face beneath them suddenly looked startlingly familiar. It was the face of Jack Stapleton, and Holmes understood at last that the naturalist carried the Baskerville blood.

Inspector Lestrade arrived from London with the quiet confidence of a man who had been summoned to complete an arrest, and Holmes unfolded his plan over supper. Sir Henry would dine at Merripit House with the Stapletons and walk home across the moor alone, as he had done before, while the three friends waited in the darkness. It was a dangerous bait, but it was the only way to catch the culprit in the act.

On the appointed night the three men crouched among the rocks near Merripit House, wrapped in their coats, while a thick white fog began to creep toward them from the direction of Grimpen Mire. It rose steadily across the low ground until the house was a dim yellow glimmer and the path to Baskerville Hall had vanished altogether. Holmes, who had counted on a clear moon, muttered a curse, for the fog was a danger that no one could have planned for.

At last a door opened in the house, and Sir Henry stepped out into the cold and set off along the path that led home across the moor, walking with a deliberate, steady stride. His steps grew fainter as the fog thickened around him, until the watchers could hear him but could hardly see him. Holmes gripped his revolver and held his breath, for every instinct told him that the enemy was close.

Then, with a sudden, deafening cry from the dark, an enormous black hound burst out of the fog and sprang along the path after Sir Henry. Its eyes glowed with a ghastly fire, its jaws were wreathed in flame, and its size was such that it seemed more a creature of nightmare than of nature. Sir Henry, with a shout of horror, threw himself forward and ran for his life, with the monster bounding behind him.

Holmes, Watson and Lestrade sprang from their hiding place and ran toward the pair, and in that instant Holmes lifted his revolver and fired shot after shot into the beast's flank. With a last howl the great animal leaped into the air and rolled over on the grass, and then it lay still. Sir Henry lay on the ground nearby, white as paper and shaking, but not a mark was upon him.

A closer look showed the thing to be a magnificent but quite ordinary hound, part bloodhound and part mastiff, though its muzzle and neck had been smeared with some preparation that shone with a pale flame. The substance was phosphorus, and its glow in the fog had been enough to turn a living animal into a spectre of the old legend. There was nothing supernatural here, Holmes said, only a cunning human mind that had understood how far fear could be made to carry.

Leaving the dead creature on the path, the men hurried to Merripit House and forced their way in, where they found no sign of its owner. In an upstairs room, bound to a post with strips of sheet, they found Beryl Stapleton, exhausted but alive. She was not Stapleton's sister at all, as they now learned, but his wife, and he had bound her there because she had refused to take part in his scheme.

Stapleton himself had fled, and only one road remained open to him on that blind night, the hidden path through Grimpen Mire that he alone knew. Holmes and Watson plunged into the fog after him, calling and listening, but the whiteness swallowed every sound. They were forced to wait for daylight, knowing that the man they hunted had every advantage of knowledge.

By daylight Holmes found Stapleton's footprints and followed them to the edge of the Mire, where the little wands that marked the safe path led out into green slime. There the tracks stopped, and near them lay Sir Henry's old black boot, thrown away like a useless tool. No body was ever found, and Holmes concluded that the Mire had swallowed the man who knew it best, though no one could say so for certain.

Back at the Hall, over a warm fire the next evening, Holmes laid out the whole history of the case for his two friends and for Dr Mortimer. Jack Stapleton, he explained, had been born a Baskerville, the son of Sir Charles's youngest brother, and with only two lives standing between him and the Hall he had settled on a murderous plan. He had returned to Devonshire under a false name, posed as a naturalist on the edge of the moor, and waited for his chance.

The hound, he continued, was a huge dog that Stapleton had bought and kept hidden in an old mine in the heart of the Mire, where it was fed and trained to hunt by scent. On the night of Sir Charles's death he had sent it along the yew alley, and the old man's weak heart had failed in sheer terror at the sight of the glowing beast. Later it was given the scent of a boot stolen from Sir Henry's hotel, and the luckless Selden, who wore Sir Henry's old clothes, had been pursued by it in his place.

Sir Henry, whose nerves had suffered terribly in that fog, was weak and silent for many days, and Dr Mortimer insisted that he rest in the quiet of the Hall. Slowly, with the help of his friends and the kind care of Barrymore and his wife, the young man began to recover his colour and his spirits. By the end of the week he could even laugh at the thought of the black hound that had once seemed to hold the whole district in its jaws.

As soon as he was strong enough, Sir Henry resolved to travel, and he and Dr Mortimer set off on a long voyage around the world to put the shadows of Baskerville Hall behind them. Before they left, he took Holmes and Watson by the hand and thanked them with a warmth that words could hardly carry. The moor, for its part, was left to the wind, the ponies and the mist, and the family curse was finally at an end.

Their work finished, Holmes and Watson returned to London, where the rattle of cabs and the glow of the streetlamps seemed wonderfully ordinary after the silence of the moor. The mystery of the hound had cost them weeks of anxiety and many sleepless nights, and it had ended in a triumph that Holmes accepted with a shrug. Behind them the people of Devonshire could walk on the moor once more, free at last of the creature that had darkened their evenings for so long.

On a damp, foggy evening at Baker Street, Holmes laid his pipe aside, stretched out his legs toward the fire, and announced with a smile that he had two tickets for the opera. Watson, who had not seen his friend so relaxed for weeks, laughed aloud and reached for his coat. The great detective had earned his rest, and, as the cab carried them through the lamplit streets, the dark moor seemed very far away.
